Exp 1 Basic Components of a Computer, Von Neumann Architecture, Number Systems, and Data Representation CO1
Monday · 27 July 2026 · 8:00 AM - 10:00 AM

Basic components of a computer

✨ The Vibe

Your computer is basically a group chat: input devices are people sending messages, output devices show the replies, memory is the chat history, and the CPU is the one actually reading messages and deciding what to reply.

📌 What you need to know
  • A computer system consists of input, output, memory, control, and ALU units.
  • The CPU processes instructions while memory stores data and programs.
  • Input and output devices connect the computer to the outside world.
  • The motherboard holds the major components and provides communication paths between them.
  • The speed of a computer depends on processor performance, memory capacity, and bus design.
💬 Talk It Out

Which everyday device do you own that's basically a mini computer with all five units packed in? Debate it with your group and defend your pick.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • A computer has five core units: input, output, memory, control unit, and ALU.
  • The control unit sequences instruction execution; the ALU performs the actual calculations.
  • Memory stores both the running program and its data.
  • Overall speed depends on processor performance, memory capacity, and bus design together, not any one factor alone.
📝 Deep Dive

Think of the computer as five cooperating units: the ALU does the arithmetic, the control unit sequences everything, memory holds data and instructions, and input/output units are the bridge to the user. On the exam, be ready to label a block diagram of these units and explain the direction of data flow between them (see Figure 1.1). Also note the difference between primary memory (RAM, fast, volatile, directly addressed by the CPU) and secondary storage (hard disk/SSD, slower, non-volatile, holds files when the computer is off) — a common point of confusion for first-year students.

🧩 Code Challenge

Draw and label the block diagram of a basic computer, then explain the role of each unit in one line.

Tap to reveal the solution

Redraw Figure 1.1 from memory. Label the five units and write, next to each: Input — accepts data from outside (keyboard, sensor); Output — presents results (monitor, printer); Memory — stores program and data together; Control Unit — sequences instruction execution; ALU — performs arithmetic and logical operations. This labeling exercise is the 'solved' form of the practice task since it has no C code — the deliverable is a correctly annotated diagram.

  3. Compare clock speed, number of cores, and cache size, and explain how each one affects overall computer speed.

Tuesday · 28 July 2026 · 2:00 PM - 4:00 PM

Von Neumann architecture and stored program model

✨ The Vibe

Keeping instructions and data in the same memory is like keeping your to-do list and your random notes in the same notes app — convenient, but also exactly how a stray 'note' can accidentally get executed as a 'to-do' (hello, security bugs).

📌 What you need to know
  • The same memory stores both data and instructions.
  • The CPU executes programs using the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
  • The architecture is the basis of most general-purpose computers.
  • The stored program model allows a computer to change behavior by loading a different program.
  • This model explains why programs can be saved, copied, and executed from memory.
💬 Talk It Out

If you were designing a new computer architecture today, would you keep instructions and data together or split them apart like Harvard architecture does? Defend your answer to your group.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • The stored-program model keeps both instructions and data in the same memory.
  • Every instruction passes through fetch, decode, and execute stages, driven by the Program Counter.
  • This model is why software can be changed simply by loading a different program into memory.
  • The Harvard architecture is a contrasting design that keeps instruction and data memory physically separate.
📝 Deep Dive

Walk through the fetch-decode-execute cycle step by step: the program counter points to the next instruction, the control unit fetches it from memory, decodes the opcode, and the ALU or control unit executes it before the cycle repeats (Figure 1.2). Contrast this with the Harvard architecture, which keeps instruction and data memory separate, to understand why Von Neumann's shared-memory design is significant. A well-known consequence of the shared-memory design is the 'Von Neumann bottleneck' — since instructions and data travel over the same bus, the CPU can be left waiting for memory even though it can compute much faster, which is why caches exist.

🧩 Code Challenge

Trace the fetch-decode-execute cycle for three sequential instructions: LOAD R1,A ; ADD R1,B ; STORE R1,C.

Tap to reveal the solution

Instruction 1 — Fetch: PC=100, control unit reads 'LOAD R1,A' from memory into the instruction register; Decode: opcode LOAD, operand A; Execute: value at address A is copied into register R1; PC becomes 101.
Instruction 2 — Fetch: reads 'ADD R1,B'; Decode: opcode ADD; Execute: ALU adds value at B to R1; PC becomes 102.
Instruction 3 — Fetch: reads 'STORE R1,C'; Decode: opcode STORE; Execute: value in R1 is written to address C; PC becomes 103.
This three-step trace is exactly what the CPU repeats for every instruction in any C program after compilation.

🎯 Try These On Your Own
  1. Explain in your own words what the Program Counter (PC) does and why it must be updated every cycle.
  2. Describe one real consequence of the stored-program model — for example, why a virus can spread by being 'data' that later gets executed as 'instructions'.
  3. Compare the Von Neumann and Harvard architectures in a short table (shared vs. separate memory, typical use).

1. In the fetch-decode-execute cycle, which stage happens first?

2. What does the Program Counter (PC) hold?

Friday · 31 July 2026 · 8:00 AM - 10:00 AM

Binary and hexadecimal systems; conversions; data representation

✨ The Vibe

Binary is just the computer speaking in yes/no, over and over. Hex is our shorthand so humans don't have to read 32 zeros and ones every time — kind of like using an emoji instead of typing a whole sentence.

📌 What you need to know
  • Positional (weighted) notation: a digit's value = digit x base^position; positions count 0, 1, 2, ... leftward from the point and -1, -2, ... rightward.
  • Binary uses two digits (0, 1); octal uses eight (0-7); decimal uses ten (0-9); hexadecimal uses sixteen (0-9, A-F, where A-F = 10-15).
  • To convert decimal to another base: divide repeatedly by the base and read the remainders bottom-to-top; for fractions, multiply repeatedly and read the integer bits top-to-bottom.
  • Binary converts directly to octal by grouping bits in 3s, and to hexadecimal by grouping bits in 4s — no decimal step needed (and the reverse: expand each octal/hex digit back to its fixed-width binary group).
  • A nibble is 4 bits and is commonly represented by one hexadecimal digit; two nibbles make a byte, which is why hex pairs like 0xAD map neatly onto byte values.
  • Data can represent integers, floating-point values, characters, images, audio, and video — each with its own bit-storage rules.
💬 Talk It Out

Your camera roll is full of photos and videos — why are video files so much bigger than photos? Connect your answer to bits-per-pixel and frames-per-second.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • Positional notation: value = sum of (digit x base^position); it's why 1011(base 2), 153(base 8), and 6B(base 16) all equal 107(base 10).
  • Decimal to another base: divide repeatedly and read remainders bottom-to-top; decimal fraction to another base: multiply repeatedly and read integer bits top-to-bottom.
  • Binary <-> octal/hex skips decimal entirely — group bits in 3s for octal, 4s for hex (and reverse: expand each digit to its fixed-width binary group).
  • A nibble is 4 bits; a byte is 8 bits (two nibbles), which is why hex pairs like 0xAD map neatly to bytes.
  • Image storage scales with bit depth per pixel: 1 bit (B/W), 8 bits (grayscale), 24 bits (RGB).
  • Audio and video storage scales with sampling rate, bit depth, and (for video) frame rate.
📝 Deep Dive

Positional notation is the foundation: for a number ...d2 d1 d0 . d-1 d-2..., Value = sum(digit x base^position). Converting to decimal just applies this directly — 1011(base 2) = (1x2^3)+(0x2^2)+(1x2^1)+(1x2^0) = 8+0+2+1 = 11(base 10); 153(base 8) = (1x8^2)+(5x8^1)+(3x8^0) = 64+40+3 = 107(base 10); 6B(base 16) = (6x16^1)+(11x16^0) = 96+11 = 107(base 10) (B = 11). Going the other way — decimal to any base — use repeated division by the target base, collecting remainders, then read them bottom-to-top (the last remainder becomes the leftmost, most-significant digit): 107 divided by 2 repeatedly gives remainders 1,1,0,1,0,1,1 (bottom-to-top), so 107(base 10) = 1101011(base 2); the same 107 divided by 8 gives 153(base 8), and divided by 16 gives 6B(base 16) — notice these are the same three numbers used above, just worked in reverse. For a fractional decimal, multiply repeatedly by the target base instead and read the integer part of each result top-to-bottom: 0.625 x 2 = 1.25 (bit 1), 0.25 x 2 = 0.5 (bit 0), 0.5 x 2 = 1.0 (bit 1), giving 0.625(base 10) = 0.101(base 2). Because 8 = 2^3 and 16 = 2^4, you can skip decimal entirely when converting between binary and octal/hex: pad the binary number to a multiple of 3 (for octal) or 4 (for hex) from the left, then convert each group independently — 1101011(base 2) padded to 001 101 011 gives octal 1-5-3 = 153(base 8), and padded to 0110 1011 gives hex 6-B = 6B(base 16). Reverse the process (octal/hex to binary) by expanding each digit back to its fixed-width group and dropping leading zeros. Keep a mental quick-reference for 0-15 in all four bases (0000=0, ..., 1001=9, 1010=A, 1011=B, 1100=C, 1101=D, 1110=E, 1111=F) since it makes hex-binary conversion almost instant. For data representation, connect each media type to a concrete number: a 100x100 black-and-white image needs 10,000 bits; the same image in 256-level grayscale needs 80,000 bits (10,000 x 8); in 24-bit RGB it needs 240,000 bits (10,000 x 24) — this is why colour images are much larger than grayscale or black-and-white ones, and why audio/video compression formats (MP3, MP4) exist. Audio is captured by sampling a continuous sound wave at fixed time intervals (sampling rate) and storing each sample as a fixed number of bits (bit depth); CD-quality sound uses a 44,100 Hz sampling rate with 16-bit depth per channel, and doubling either value roughly doubles the storage needed per second. Video is a fast sequence of still frames played with a synchronized audio stream; more frames per second (fps) gives smoother motion but needs more storage. ASCII uses 7-bit character codes, while Unicode supports a much larger set of symbols.

🧩 Code Challenge

Convert 173 (decimal) to binary, octal, and hexadecimal; write a C program that verifies the answer using printf format specifiers, and calculate storage for a 4x4 grayscale image.

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
int main(){
    int n = 173;
    printf("Decimal     : %d\n", n);
    printf("Octal       : %o\n", n);
    printf("Hexadecimal : %x\n", n);
    // Manual binary conversion using bitwise checks
    printf("Binary      : ");
    for (int bit = 7; bit >= 0; bit--)
        printf("%d", (n >> bit) & 1);
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
Decimal     : 173
Octal       : 255
Hexadecimal : ad
Binary      : 10101101

Storage check: a 4x4 grayscale image has 16 pixels x 8 bits/pixel = 128 bits = 16 bytes.

  2. Convert 11001101 (binary) to decimal, octal, and hexadecimal.
  3. Convert 0.375 (decimal) to binary using repeated multiplication (fractional conversion).
  4. Calculate the storage (in bits and bytes) needed for a 4x4 black-and-white image, the same image in 256-level grayscale, and the same image in 24-bit RGB.

Exp 2 Flowcharts, Pseudocode, and Problem-Solving CO2
Monday · 03 August 2026 · 8:00 AM - 10:00 AM

Flowcharts and pseudocode

✨ The Vibe

A flowchart is basically the storyboard for a video before you film it — you plan the shot list (the logic) first, then 'filming' the algorithm in C is the easy part.

📌 What you need to know
  • Flowcharts visually represent algorithm steps.
  • Pseudocode expresses logic in structured plain language.
  • Both help plan a solution before coding.
  • Standard flowchart symbols include terminator, input/output, process, and decision.
  • Pseudocode should be clear enough that it can be directly converted into code.
💬 Talk It Out

Explain your even/odd flowchart out loud to a partner without using any code words at all — like you're explaining it to a friend who's never coded.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • A flowchart is the visual map of an algorithm; pseudocode is its plain-language, step-by-step description.
  • Standard symbols (terminator, input/output, process, decision) keep flowcharts consistent and readable.
  • Pseudocode should be detailed enough to translate almost line-by-line into real code.
  • Always plan the flowchart/pseudocode before writing any C code.
📝 Deep Dive

A flowchart and its pseudocode should always describe exactly the same logic — think of the flowchart as the 'map' and the pseudocode as the 'turn-by-turn directions'. When you later translate pseudocode into C (as in the worked solution below), each pseudocode line usually becomes one or two C statements, which is why writing careful pseudocode first makes coding much faster and less error-prone.

🧩 Code Challenge

Write pseudocode, draw a flowchart, and implement a C program to check whether a number is even or odd.

Tap to reveal the solution

The pseudocode above (START/READ/IF.../STOP) is translated line-by-line into the C program below — this is exactly the mapping you should practice for every new problem.

START
READ n
remainder = n MOD 2
IF remainder == 0 THEN
    PRINT "Even"
ELSE
    PRINT "Odd"
ENDIF
STOP
C Program:
#include <stdio.h>
int main(){
    int n;
    printf("Enter a number: ");
    scanf("%d", &n);
    if (n % 2 == 0) printf("Even\n");
    else printf("Odd\n");
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
Enter a number: 7
Odd
🎯 Try These On Your Own

  2. Write pseudocode and a flowchart to convert a temperature from Celsius to Fahrenheit.
  3. Write pseudocode and a flowchart to check whether a character entered by the user is a vowel or a consonant.

Tuesday · 04 August 2026 · 2:00 PM - 4:00 PM

Problem-solving strategies

✨ The Vibe

Problem-solving strategies are basically your study playlist for hard problems: warm up with examples, reverse-engineer from the goal (like reverse-engineering a recipe from the finished dish), and break the big scary problem into bite-sized chunks.

📌 What you need to know
  • Use examples to understand the problem.
  • Work backwards from the goal if the path is unclear.
  • Break the task into smaller parts.
  • Study similarities between a new problem and an already solved problem.
  • Good problem solving begins with identifying inputs, outputs, and constraints.
💬 Talk It Out

Pick a problem you got stuck on this week in ANY class, and identify which of the five strategies from this session would have helped.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • Identify inputs, outputs, and constraints before attempting any solution.
  • Working backwards from the goal often reveals what intermediate steps are needed.
  • Breaking a big problem into smaller sub-problems makes each part easier to solve and test.
  • Recognizing similarities with previously solved problems saves time and effort.
📝 Deep Dive

Before writing any code, get into the habit of writing down: what is given (inputs), what is required (outputs), and any limits on the values (constraints). This three-part framing prevents wasted effort and is the same discipline used in competitive programming and technical interviews. When a problem feels too big, break it into two or three smaller sub-problems that are each easy to solve on their own — this is the same top-down thinking used later in Experiment 4.

🧩 Code Challenge

Apply the input-output-constraint framework to the problem 'find the average of n student marks'.

Tap to reveal the solution

Inputs: n (number of students), followed by n integer marks. Output: the average as a floating-point value. Constraints: n must be greater than 0 (avoid division by zero); marks are typically between 0 and 100. Working backwards from the output (average = sum / n) tells you that you need an accumulator variable for the sum and a loop that runs exactly n times — this is the plan you would code directly in the next experiment.

  3. Write down the inputs, outputs, and constraints for the problem 'check if a given year is a leap year'.

Friday · 07 August 2026 · 8:00 AM - 10:00 AM

C compilation process; syntax and semantic errors

✨ The Vibe

A compiler catching a syntax error is like autocorrect catching an obvious typo instantly. A semantic error is when autocorrect 'fixes' your text into something that reads fine grammatically but says the completely wrong thing.

📌 What you need to know
  • Compilation converts source code into executable form.
  • Syntax errors break language rules.
  • Semantic errors are logic errors that produce wrong results.
  • The preprocessing stage handles directives such as #include and #define.
  • Linking combines object files and library code into one executable.
💬 Talk It Out

Share a real autocorrect fail with your group and vote on whether it counts as a 'syntax' or 'semantic' error.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • Compilation proceeds through preprocessing, compilation, assembly, linking, and loading.
  • Syntax errors break language rules and stop compilation; semantic errors compile fine but give wrong results.
  • The preprocessor handles #include and #define before the compiler ever sees the code.
  • Linking combines object files and libraries into one final executable.
📝 Deep Dive

The full pipeline is: preprocessing (macro expansion, header inclusion) -> compilation (source to assembly/object code) -> assembly -> linking (combining object files and libraries into one executable) -> loading (placing the executable in memory to run). A missing semicolon is a syntax error the compiler catches; using + instead of * is a semantic error the compiler will not catch. As a rule of thumb: if the compiler refuses to produce an executable at all, it is almost certainly a syntax error; if the program compiles and runs but gives a wrong answer, it is a semantic (logic) error that only testing can reveal.

🧩 Code Challenge

Identify and fix one syntax error and one semantic error in a short program.

Tap to reveal the solution 
// Faulty version:
// #include <stdio.h>
// int main(){
//     int a = 5, b = 3
//     int area = a + b;   // syntax error: missing ';' after b
//                          // semantic error: should be a * b for 'area'
//     printf("%d\n", area);
//     return 0;
// }

// Corrected version:
#include <stdio.h>
int main(){
    int a = 5, b = 3;
    int area = a * b;
    printf("%d\n", area);
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
15

  3. List, in order, the five stages a C source file passes through before it becomes a running program.

Exp 3 Variables, Data Types, Operators, and Expressions CO3
Monday · 10 August 2026 · 8:00 AM - 10:00 AM

Variable names, data types and sizes, constants, declarations

✨ The Vibe

Data types are like playlist categories — you wouldn't drop a video file into your audio-only playlist. C wants you to be just as specific about what kind of value a variable is allowed to hold.

📌 What you need to know
  • Meaningful names improve readability.
  • Different data types store different kinds of values.
  • Constants and declarations define program data clearly.
  • Variable names should not start with digits and should avoid reserved keywords.
  • The size of a type may vary by compiler, so using sizeof is helpful.
💬 Talk It Out

Debate this: should C have just one generic data type instead of int/float/char/etc.? What would we actually lose?

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • C's basic types are char, int, float, and double, modifiable with short/long/signed/unsigned.
  • Always use sizeof rather than assuming a fixed byte size for a type.
  • Use meaningful variable names; avoid starting names with digits or using reserved keywords.
  • Declare constants with #define or const so fixed values are clear and cannot be changed accidentally.
📝 Deep Dive

C has a small set of basic types — char, int, float, and double — and each can be modified with short, long, signed, or unsigned to change its range and size. Since the exact byte size of int or long can differ between compilers and machines, always use the sizeof operator instead of assuming a fixed size; this habit avoids subtle bugs when code is moved between systems. A constant declared with const or #define should be used for any fixed value (like the number of days in a week) so its meaning is clear and it cannot be accidentally changed later in the program.

🧩 Code Challenge

Declare and print variables for temperature (float), area (double), and an initial letter (char), and print the size of each type using sizeof.

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
int main(){
    float temperature = 36.6f;
    double area = 452.389;
    char initial = 'R';
    printf("Temperature = %.1f (size %zu bytes)\n", temperature, sizeof(temperature));
    printf("Area = %.3f (size %zu bytes)\n", area, sizeof(area));
    printf("Initial = %c (size %zu byte)\n", initial, sizeof(initial));
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
Temperature = 36.6 (size 4 bytes)
Area = 452.389 (size 8 bytes)
Initial = R (size 1 byte)

  3. List three invalid C variable names (for example, one starting with a digit, one using a reserved keyword) and explain why each is invalid.

Tuesday · 11 August 2026 · 2:00 PM - 4:00 PM

Arithmetic, relational, logical, and bitwise operators

✨ The Vibe

Bitwise vs. logical operators is the ultimate mix-up, like & vs && — one compares things bit by bit, the other just asks a single 'is this whole thing true or not' question.

📌 What you need to know
  • Arithmetic operators perform calculations.
  • Relational and logical operators are used for decisions.
  • Bitwise operators work at the binary level.
  • Operator precedence controls which operation is evaluated first.
  • Logical operators return true or false-like values based on conditions.
💬 Talk It Out

In pairs, explain the difference between & and && using a real, non-coding yes/no example from everyday life.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • Relational operators (>, <, ==, etc.) always evaluate to 1 (true) or 0 (false) in C.
  • Logical operators (&&, ||, !) short-circuit — the second operand may not even be evaluated.
  • Bitwise operators (&, |, ^, ~, <<, >>) act on individual bits and are unrelated to logical operators.
  • Operator precedence determines evaluation order — multiplication/division bind tighter than addition/subtraction.
📝 Deep Dive

Relational operators (>, <, ==, !=, >=, <=) always produce 1 (true) or 0 (false) in C — there is no separate boolean type in classic C. Logical operators (&&, ||, !) combine these true/false results and short-circuit: in (a > 0 && b > 0), if a > 0 is false, C does not even evaluate b > 0, which matters if the second expression has side effects. Bitwise operators (&, |, ^, ~, <<, >>) act on the individual bits of a number and are unrelated to logical operators, even though & looks similar to &&; mixing them up is one of the most common beginner mistakes.

🧩 Code Challenge

Write a program that demonstrates operator precedence (2 + 3 * 4) and bitwise AND/OR on 12 and 10.

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
int main(){
    int result = 2 + 3 * 4;         // * evaluated before +
    int a = 12, b = 10;
    printf("2 + 3 * 4 = %d\n", result);
    printf("12 & 10 = %d\n", a & b);
    printf("12 | 10 = %d\n", a | b);
    printf("12 ^ 10 = %d\n", a ^ b);
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
2 + 3 * 4 = 14
12 & 10 = 8
12 | 10 = 14
12 ^ 10 = 6

  2. Use the left-shift (<<) and right-shift (>>) operators on the value 5 and predict the results before running the program.
  3. Explain, with an example, the difference between & (bitwise AND) and && (logical AND).

Friday · 14 August 2026 · 8:00 AM - 10:00 AM

Type conversions, increment/decrement, assignment, conditional expressions, precedence

✨ The Vibe

Post-increment vs. pre-increment is basically 'read the message, then mark it as read' vs. 'mark it as read, then show me the updated view' — same action, different order changes what you actually see.

📌 What you need to know
  • Type conversion may happen automatically or by casting.
  • Increment and decrement change values by 1.
  • Operator precedence controls evaluation order.
  • Pre-increment changes the value before use, while post-increment changes it after use.
  • The conditional operator can replace a short if-else in simple expressions.
💬 Talk It Out

Predict together what a++ + ++a would print for a starting value, then run it and see who called it correctly.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • Implicit conversion happens automatically when mixing types; explicit casting, like (float)x, is done intentionally.
  • Pre-increment (++a) changes the value before it is used; post-increment (a++) changes it after.
  • Compound assignment operators (+=, -=, *=, /=) are shorthand for 'apply the operator and store back'.
  • The conditional operator (cond ? a : b) is an expression with a value, usable inside printf or assignments.
📝 Deep Dive

Implicit type conversion happens automatically when C combines two different types in one expression (an int is 'promoted' to float when added to a float); explicit casting, like (float)x, is used when you want that conversion to happen intentionally at a specific point, such as before a division to avoid truncation. Compound assignment operators (+=, -=, *=, /=) are shorthand for 'take the variable, apply the operator, and store it back' — x += 5 means exactly x = x + 5. The conditional operator cond ? a : b is an expression (it has a value), not a statement, so it can be used directly inside printf or an assignment.

🧩 Code Challenge

Use explicit casting to compute the average of two integers as a float, and use the conditional operator to print the larger value.

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
int main(){
    int x = 7, y = 4;
    float avg = (float)(x + y) / 2;   // cast prevents integer division
    int larger = (x > y) ? x : y;      // conditional operator
    printf("Average = %.2f\n", avg);
    printf("Larger value = %d\n", larger);
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
Average = 5.50
Larger value = 7
🎯 Try These On Your Own
  1. Predict, then verify, the output of int x = 5; printf("%d %d %d", x++, x, ++x);
  2. Write a program that uses compound assignment operators (+=, -=, *=) to update a running total.
  3. Use the conditional operator to print 'Pass' or 'Fail' based on whether marks are at least 40.

1. What does (float)(x + y) / 2 accomplish compared to (x + y) / 2 when x, y are int?

2. What is printed by: int a = 5; printf("%d", ++a);

Statements and blocks; if-else and else-if

✨ The Vibe

An if-else-if ladder is your group chat's decision tree for 'what are we eating tonight' — check the strongest preference first and stop as soon as one hits.

📌 What you need to know
  • A block groups multiple statements.
  • if-else handles two-way selection.
  • else-if ladders handle multiple conditions.
  • Indentation helps make the flow easy to read.
  • Nested if statements are useful when one decision depends on another.
💬 Talk It Out

Design an if-else ladder out loud for deciding your Friday night plans based on mood, budget, and who's actually free.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • if-else handles two-way decisions; else-if ladders handle multiple ordered conditions.
  • else always binds to the nearest unmatched if — consistent indentation avoids confusion, even though C ignores whitespace.
  • An else-if ladder stops at the first true condition, so order conditions from most to least specific.
  • Nested ifs should generally be limited to two or three levels before refactoring for clarity.
📝 Deep Dive

An else always binds to the nearest unmatched if, which is why consistent indentation matters even though C ignores whitespace — misleading indentation can make a program look correct while behaving differently. An else-if ladder is evaluated top to bottom, and execution stops at the first condition that is true, so order the conditions carefully (for example, check the highest grade boundary first, then work downward). Nested if statements should generally be limited to two or three levels deep; beyond that, the logic usually becomes easier to read as a combination of logical operators or a switch statement.

🧩 Code Challenge

Write a program to assign a grade from marks (A: >=90, B: >=75, C: >=60, else D) and a program to check if a year is a leap year.

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
int main(){
    int marks = 82;
    char grade;
    if (marks >= 90) grade = 'A';
    else if (marks >= 75) grade = 'B';
    else if (marks >= 60) grade = 'C';
    else grade = 'D';
    printf("Grade = %c\n", grade);

    int year = 2028;
    if ((year % 4 == 0 && year % 100 != 0) || year % 400 == 0)
        printf("%d is a leap year\n", year);
    else
        printf("%d is not a leap year\n", year);
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
Grade = B
2028 is a leap year

Tuesday · 18 August 2026 · 2:00 PM - 4:00 PM

Switch; top-down design and breaking problems into sub-problems

✨ The Vibe

switch is basically your phone's 'allow notifications except for these apps' list — it only matches exact values, it can't handle a whole range like 'anything between 60 and 100.'

📌 What you need to know
  • Switch is suitable for one-variable case-based selection.
  • Top-down design begins with the whole problem.
  • Sub-problems make programming easier.
  • A menu-driven program is a good example of switch-based design.
  • A proper structure helps separate input handling, decision logic, and output.
💬 Talk It Out

Why can't switch directly handle 'if marks are between 60 and 100' the way if-else can? Talk it through with a partner.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • switch tests one variable for equality against constant case values only — it cannot test ranges.
  • Always include break at the end of each case, unless intentional fall-through is desired.
  • Top-down design starts from the whole problem and repeatedly splits it into smaller sub-problems.
  • A menu-driven program is a natural application of switch-based, top-down design.
📝 Deep Dive

A switch statement only tests equality of one variable against constant values, so it cannot replace an if that tests ranges (like marks >= 90); this is the key criterion for choosing switch over if-else. Always remember break at the end of each case — without it, execution 'falls through' into the next case, which is occasionally useful (for grouping cases) but usually a bug. Top-down design means starting from the full problem statement and repeatedly splitting it into smaller, independent sub-problems until each piece is small enough to write as a single function — this is exactly how the calculator below separates 'get the choice' from 'perform the operation'.

🧩 Code Challenge

Extend the calculator switch with modulus (case 3) and power (case 4, using a loop instead of math.h).

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
int main(){
    int ch = 4, a = 2, b = 5;
    int result = 1;
    switch (ch){
        case 1: printf("%d\n", a + b); break;
        case 2: printf("%d\n", a - b); break;
        case 3: printf("%d\n", a % b); break;
        case 4:
            for (int i = 0; i < b; i++) result *= a;
            printf("%d\n", result);
            break;
        default: printf("Invalid\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
32
🎯 Try These On Your Own
  1. Write a switch-based program that prints the name of the day of the week for a number 1-7 (1=Monday, ... 7=Sunday).
  2. Write a menu-driven program using switch that lets the user choose to calculate the area of a circle, rectangle, or triangle.
  3. Deliberately remove one 'break' statement from a working switch program, run it, and explain the fall-through behaviour you observe.

Friday · 21 August 2026 · 8:00 AM - 10:00 AM

Loops: while, for, do-while; break, continue; goto and labels

✨ The Vibe

for vs. while vs. do-while is basically 'I know exactly how many stories I'm posting today' vs. 'I'll keep posting until I run out of content' vs. 'I'm posting at least once no matter what.'

📌 What you need to know
  • Loops are used when a statement must be repeated until a condition changes.
  • while and for are entry-controlled; do-while is exit-controlled.
  • break and continue modify loop flow.
  • Loops usually need initialization, condition, and update steps.
  • A loop becomes infinite if the termination condition is never reached.
💬 Talk It Out

Come up with your own everyday example for each of the three loop types and share with your group.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • for suits a known number of repetitions; while suits condition-driven repetition; do-while runs its body at least once.
  • break exits a loop immediately; continue skips only the rest of the current iteration.
  • A loop needs initialization, a condition, and an update step to avoid running forever.
  • goto exists in C but is rarely used because it can make control flow hard to follow.
📝 Deep Dive

Choose for when you know the number of repetitions in advance (it keeps initialization, condition, and update together on one line), and while when the number of repetitions depends on a condition discovered during the loop. A do-while always executes its body at least once before checking the condition, which is useful for input-validation menus that must run at least one time. break exits the loop immediately, while continue skips only the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next one; goto is rarely used in modern C because it can make control flow hard to follow, but it is occasionally used to break out of deeply nested loops in one step.

🧩 Code Challenge

Print numbers from 1 to 10, skipping multiples of 3 using continue, and stopping the loop entirely once the number 8 is reached using break.

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
int main(){
    for (int i = 1; i <= 10; i++){
        if (i % 3 == 0) continue;   // skip multiples of 3
        if (i == 8) break;          // stop the loop at 8
        printf("%d ", i);
    }
    printf("\n");
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
1 2 4 5 7

  2. Write a program using a for loop to print the multiplication table of a given number from 1 to 10.
  3. Write a program that uses nested for loops to print a right-angled triangle pattern of stars (5 rows).

Implementation of algorithms and modularity

✨ The Vibe

Functions are like saving a filter preset on a camera app — build the exact adjustment once, then reuse it instantly instead of re-adjusting from scratch every single time.

📌 What you need to know
  • Modularity divides the solution into smaller units.
  • Functions reduce repetition.
  • Clear structure improves testing and reuse.
  • A modular program is easier to debug because each part can be checked separately.
  • Procedure-like decomposition helps make larger solutions manageable.
💬 Talk It Out

Pick a repetitive task from your daily routine and describe out loud how you'd 'functionize' it.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • Modularity divides a solution into smaller, independently testable units.
  • Each function should do exactly one job, described clearly by its name.
  • Building a program from small functions mirrors the top-down design approach.
  • Modular programs are easier to debug because each function can be verified in isolation.
📝 Deep Dive

A function should ideally do exactly one job, described by its name — sumArray sums, averageArray averages — and larger jobs are built by calling several small functions from main rather than writing one long block of code. This mirrors top-down design from Experiment 4: once a problem is broken into sub-problems, each sub-problem usually becomes one function. Modularity also makes testing much easier, because each function can be tested on its own with a few sample inputs before it is combined with the rest of the program.

🧩 Code Challenge

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
int sumArray(int arr[], int n){
    int total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) total += arr[i];
    return total;
}
float averageArray(int arr[], int n){
    return (float)sumArray(arr, n) / n;
}
int main(){
    int marks[5] = {80, 90, 70, 85, 95};
    printf("Sum = %d\n", sumArray(marks, 5));
    printf("Average = %.2f\n", averageArray(marks, 5));
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
Sum = 420
Average = 84.00

Choice of variable names; documentation; debugging

✨ The Vibe

Good variable names and comments are basically writing captions people can actually understand without you standing there explaining the joke afterward.

📌 What you need to know
  • Good names improve readability.
  • Comments should explain intent, not obvious syntax.
  • Debugging is the process of locating and fixing mistakes.
  • Documentation should explain inputs, outputs, and assumptions.
  • A good debug habit is to test with one small case first and then expand.
💬 Talk It Out

Swap code with a partner and honestly rate each other's variable names — brutal but fair only.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • Meaningful variable names make code self-documenting and easier to maintain.
  • Comments should explain intent (why), not restate what the code obviously already says.
  • Debug by isolating the smallest failing case and changing one thing at a time.
  • A good header comment states a function's inputs, assumptions, and expected output.
📝 Deep Dive

Prefer a name like studentCount over a bare n when the meaning matters. When debugging, isolate the smallest failing case, add print statements or use a debugger to inspect variable values at each step, and change one thing at a time so you know which change fixed the issue. A comment like // increment i is useless because it repeats what the code already says; a useful comment explains why, such as // skip the header row when reading the file. Good documentation at the top of a function should state, in one or two lines, what it expects as input, what it assumes about that input (for example, 'n must be positive'), and what it returns.

🧩 Code Challenge

Debug a small program that incorrectly computes the sum of array elements due to a loop boundary mistake.

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
int main(){
    int arr[5] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
    int total = 0;
    // Bug was: for (int i = 0; i <= 5; i++)  -> reads one element past the array
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++){
        total += arr[i];
    }
    printf("Total = %d\n", total);
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
Total = 15

Debugging note: the off-by-one bug (using <= instead of <) reads memory past the array's last valid index, producing an unpredictable extra value. Testing with a small, known array (as above) makes such bugs easy to spot.

✨ The Vibe

Testing edge cases is you stress-testing a group project before presenting it — what if someone's absent, what if the wifi dies mid-demo, what if the input is zero?

📌 What you need to know
  • Testing checks normal and edge cases.
  • Functions may return different types.

📝 Deep Dive

External (global) variables are convenient for sharing state across many functions but should be used sparingly, since overusing them makes it hard to track which function changed what value and when.

Exp 6 Scope Rules, Header Files, and Storage Classes CO3
Monday · 31 August 2026 · 8:00 AM - 10:00 AM

Scope rules and block structure

✨ The Vibe

Scope is basically your close-friends list on social media — some things are visible to everyone (global), some only to whoever's inside that one specific chat (local/block scope).

📌 What you need to know
  • Scope decides where a variable is visible.
  • Blocks create local scopes.
  • Nested blocks can hide outer variables.
  • Variables declared inside a block cannot normally be used outside that block.
  • Understanding scope helps avoid naming conflicts.
💬 Talk It Out

Explain to a partner why two totally different functions can each have a local variable named 'count' without any conflict.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • Scope determines where a variable's name is valid — mainly block scope and file scope in C.
  • A variable declared in an inner block can shadow an outer variable of the same name.
  • Shadowing only affects the inner block; the outer variable is restored once that block ends.
  • Keep variables in the smallest scope that needs them to reduce naming conflicts.
📝 Deep Dive

A variable's scope is the region of the program where its name is valid; C mainly uses block scope (from the opening { to the matching }) and file scope (visible throughout a source file). When an inner block declares a variable with the same name as an outer one, the inner variable 'shadows' the outer one only within that inner block — the outer variable is untouched and reappears once the inner block ends. Keeping variables in the smallest scope that needs them (rather than always declaring at the top of main) reduces the chance of accidentally reusing a name for two different purposes.

🧩 Code Challenge

Write a program with a nested block that shadows an outer variable of the same name, and print both values to show the difference.

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
int main(){
    int x = 10;
    printf("Outer x = %d\n", x);
    {
        int x = 99;   // shadows the outer x within this block
        printf("Inner x = %d\n", x);
    }
    printf("Outer x after block = %d\n", x);
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
Outer x = 10
Inner x = 99
Outer x after block = 10

Header files and initialization

✨ The Vibe

Header files are the shared 'group chat rules' doc — everyone references the same agreed-on definitions instead of re-explaining themselves every single time.

📌 What you need to know
  • Header files carry declarations shared across source files.
  • Initialization assigns values at declaration time.
  • Well-structured programs include headers cleanly.
  • Headers often contain function prototypes and macro definitions.
  • Initialization makes the starting value of a variable explicit.
💬 Talk It Out

Why do you think large team projects — like an app built by 50 developers — rely so heavily on header files?

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • Header files hold declarations (prototypes, macros) shared across multiple .c files.
  • System headers use angle brackets (<...>); your own headers use quotes ("...").
  • Always initialize variables at declaration where possible to avoid garbage values.
  • Header files typically declare interfaces; the .c file provides the actual implementation.
📝 Deep Dive

A header file (.h) typically holds function prototypes, macro definitions, and type declarations that multiple .c files need to share, while the actual function bodies live in a corresponding .c file — this separation is what lets a large project be split across many files that still agree on each other's interfaces. Standard headers like stdio.h and math.h use angle brackets (#include <...>) because they live in the compiler's system directories; your own headers use quotes (#include "...") because they live in your project folder. Always initialize variables at the point of declaration where possible (int count = 0; rather than int count;) — an uninitialized local variable in C holds an unpredictable 'garbage' value, which is a very common source of first-year bugs.

🧩 Code Challenge

Tap to reveal the solution

#define PI 3.14159
float circleArea(float r);

// myheader.c
#include "myheader.h"
float circleArea(float r){ return PI * r * r; }

// main.c
#include <stdio.h>
#include "myheader.h"
int main(){
    printf("%.2f\n", circleArea(2.0f));
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
12.57

Friday · 04 September 2026 · 8:00 AM - 10:00 AM

Static variables and register variables

✨ The Vibe

A static variable is basically your phone's step counter — it doesn't reset every time you reopen the app, it remembers your progress.

📌 What you need to know
  • Static variables retain values between calls.
  • Register variables are compiler hints.
  • Storage classes affect lifetime and visibility.
  • A static variable is useful when a function needs to remember its previous state.
  • Register storage is mostly a request and not a guarantee.
💬 Talk It Out

Come up with a real app feature that behaves exactly like a static variable, remembering state between uses.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • C has four storage classes: auto, static, extern, and register.
  • static local variables retain their value between function calls and initialize only once.
  • register is a hint to the compiler and is mostly optimized automatically by modern compilers.
  • Storage class controls lifetime and storage location; scope still controls visibility of the name.
📝 Deep Dive

C has four storage classes — auto (the default for local variables, created and destroyed with each function call), static (keeps its value between calls and is initialized only once), extern (refers to a variable defined elsewhere, usually in another file), and register (a hint to the compiler to keep the variable in a fast CPU register, which modern compilers mostly optimize automatically). The key exam distinction is between scope (where a name is visible) and storage class (how long a variable lives and where it is stored) — a static variable inside a function still has that function's local scope, but its lifetime extends across the whole program.

🧩 Code Challenge

Write a function with both a static and an automatic (local) counter, called three times, and compare the printed values.

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
void compareCounters(void){
    static int staticCount = 0;   // retains value across calls
    int autoCount = 0;             // resets every call
    staticCount++;
    autoCount++;
    printf("static=%d automatic=%d\n", staticCount, autoCount);
}
int main(){
    compareCounters();
    compareCounters();
    compareCounters();
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
static=1 automatic=1
static=2 automatic=1
static=3 automatic=1

  • stdio.h supports basic input and output.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • printf format specifiers follow the pattern %[width].[precision][type].
  • Width sets a minimum field size (padding with spaces or zeros); precision controls decimals or max string length.

  • Escape sequences like \n, \t, and \\ embed special characters inside string literals.
📝 Deep Dive

A printf format specifier has the general form %[width].[precision][type] — width sets the minimum number of characters (padding with spaces, or zeros if you write %010.2f), and precision controls decimal places for floats or maximum characters for strings. A negative width (%-10s) left-aligns instead of the default right-alignment, which is handy for building simple text tables. Escape sequences like \n (newline), \t (tab), and \\ (a literal backslash) let you embed special characters inside an ordinary string literal.

  • scanf requires the address-of operator (&) for simple variables like scanf("%d", &n).

📝 Deep Dive

scanf requires the address-of operator (&) for simple variables, such as scanf("%d", &n) — forgetting the & is one of the most common first-year mistakes and can crash the program or silently corrupt memory. getchar() and putchar() work on a single character at a time and are the building blocks that more complex string-reading functions are built from internally. Always consider what happens with unexpected input: if scanf("%d", &n) is given a letter instead of a digit, the read fails and n keeps whatever value it had before, so production-quality code checks the return value of scanf before trusting the input.

Exp 8 Recursion and the C Preprocessor CO3
Monday · 14 September 2026 · 8:00 AM - 10:00 AM

Recursion

✨ The Vibe

Recursion is like a chain story where each character tells the next chapter to a brand-new character, until the very last one just says 'the end' (the base case) — then everyone reports their part back up the chain.

📌 What you need to know
  • A function can call itself to solve a smaller problem.
  • A base case must stop recursion.
  • Recursion is common in factorial and Fibonacci problems.
  • Recursive thinking is useful when a problem is naturally defined in terms of smaller subproblems.
  • The call stack grows with each recursive call, so the stopping condition is critical.
💬 Talk It Out

Explain factorial(5) to a partner using the chain-story analogy, then trace through it together on paper.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • Every recursive function needs a base case (stops recursion) and a recursive case (reduces toward it).
  • Each recursive call adds a frame to the call stack; a missing base case causes a stack overflow.
  • Recursion is not automatically faster or more memory-efficient than a loop.
  • Recursion often produces the clearest code for problems naturally defined in terms of themselves.
📝 Deep Dive

Every recursive function needs exactly two parts: a base case that stops the recursion (fact(1) = 1) and a recursive case that reduces the problem toward the base case (fact(n) = n * fact(n-1)). Each call adds a new frame to the call stack (Figure 8.1); if the base case is missing or unreachable, the stack keeps growing until the program crashes with a stack overflow. Recursion is not always faster or more memory-efficient than a loop — naive recursive Fibonacci, for example, recomputes the same values many times — but it often produces the clearest possible code for problems that are naturally defined in terms of themselves.

🧩 Code Challenge

Write recursive functions for the nth Fibonacci number and the sum of digits of an integer.

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
int fib(int n){
    if (n == 0) return 0;
    if (n == 1) return 1;
    return fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2);
}
int sumOfDigits(int n){
    if (n == 0) return 0;
    return (n % 10) + sumOfDigits(n / 10);
}
int main(){
    printf("fib(6) = %d\n", fib(6));
    printf("sumOfDigits(1234) = %d\n", sumOfDigits(1234));
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
fib(6) = 8
sumOfDigits(1234) = 10

C preprocessor; file inclusion; macro substitution

✨ The Vibe

Macros are basically find-and-replace on steroids, done before your code even runs — like a universal autocorrect rule that swaps text everywhere it appears.

📌 What you need to know
  • The preprocessor runs before compilation.
  • Headers are included with #include.
  • Macros replace repetitive text or values.
  • Macros should be written carefully because they are expanded by text substitution.
  • Header files improve organization and reuse.
💬 Talk It Out

Why can forgetting parentheses in a macro twist the math, the same way autocorrect can twist a sentence's meaning?

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • The preprocessor performs pure text substitution before the compiler sees the code.
  • Macro parameters must be wrapped in parentheses to avoid incorrect expansion of expressions.
  • Object-like macros (#define PI 3.14159) use no memory since they vanish before compilation.
  • Macros do not respect scope or type checking, unlike real functions or const variables.
📝 Deep Dive

The preprocessor performs pure text substitution before the compiler ever sees the code, which is why macro parameters must always be wrapped in parentheses: #define SQUARE(x) ((x)*(x)) protects against surprises when x is itself an expression like a+b — without the extra parentheses, SQUARE(a+b) would expand to a+b*a+b, which is wrong. Object-like macros (#define PI 3.14159) simply substitute a name for a value and use no memory the way a variable would, since they disappear entirely before compilation. Because macros are expanded blindly, they do not respect scope or type checking, so for anything beyond simple constants, a real C function or a const variable is usually safer than a macro.

int main(){
    printf("Length = %d, Breadth = %d\n", LENGTH, BREADTH);
    printf("Area = %d\n", AREA(LENGTH, BREADTH));
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
Length = 12, Breadth = 5
Area = 60

Conditional inclusion

✨ The Vibe

#ifdef DEBUG is basically a director's commentary toggle — flip it on to see behind-the-scenes notes, flip it off for the clean final cut.

📌 What you need to know
  • Conditional compilation uses #if, #ifdef, and #ifndef.
  • It helps create version-specific code.
  • It is useful for debugging builds.
  • Conditional inclusion is often used to turn debug messages on or off.
  • These directives help compile different code paths without changing the source manually each time.
💬 Talk It Out

Where else — apps, games, settings menus — have you seen a similar 'debug mode' or 'developer options' toggle in real life?

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • #ifdef includes code only if a macro has been defined; #ifndef is the opposite.
  • #ifndef/#define/#endif 'include guards' prevent a header from being included twice.

  • Toggling a single #define DEBUG line is a lightweight way to switch diagnostics on/off.
📝 Deep Dive

#ifdef NAME includes the following code only if NAME has been #defined somewhere earlier (in the file or via a compiler flag like -DDEBUG); #ifndef is the opposite, and is most commonly seen as an 'include guard' at the top of header files to stop the same header from being included twice in one compilation. #if, unlike #ifdef, can test the actual value of a macro (#if VERSION >= 2), which is useful for maintaining slightly different code for different versions of a program from a single source file. Toggling a single #define DEBUG line on or off is a common, lightweight alternative to a full debugger for switching diagnostic output on and off.

Pointers and addresses

✨ The Vibe

A pointer is literally just someone's home address, not the person — &x hands you the address, *p is you actually walking over and knocking on the door.

📌 What you need to know
  • A pointer stores a memory address.
  • & gets an address and * dereferences a pointer.
  • Pointers are central to low-level C programming.
  • The type of the pointer should match the type of the data it points to.
  • Incorrect pointer use can cause undefined behavior.
💬 Talk It Out

Explain pointers to a partner using ONLY the 'address vs. the actual house' analogy — no code words allowed.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • A pointer stores a memory address; & gets an address, * dereferences it.
  • The pointer's declared type must match the type of data it points to.
  • Dereferencing an uninitialized or dangling pointer is undefined behaviour and must be avoided.
  • Modifying *p also modifies the original variable it points to.
📝 Deep Dive

A pointer is just a variable whose value happens to be a memory address (Figure 9.1); declaring int *p means 'p is a pointer that will hold the address of an int'. The & operator answers 'where does this variable live?' and the * operator answers 'what value lives at this address?' — used together, int *p = &x; followed by *p gives you x back. A pointer that has not been assigned a valid address (an uninitialized or 'dangling' pointer) must never be dereferenced, since doing so reads or writes to an unpredictable memory location and is one of the most serious classes of bugs in C.

🧩 Code Challenge

Declare an integer, point to it, change its value through the pointer, and print before/after values.

Tap to reveal the solution

int main(){
    int x = 20;
    int *p = &x;
    printf("Before: x = %d\n", x);
    *p = 99;               // modify x through the pointer
    printf("After : x = %d\n", x);
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
Before: x = 20
After : x = 99

Pointers and function arguments; pointers and arrays

✨ The Vibe

Passing a pointer into a function is like giving someone your house key instead of a photo of your house — now they can actually walk in and change something.

📌 What you need to know
  • Pointers let functions modify original values.
  • Arrays are closely related to pointers in function calls.
  • Pointer arithmetic can be used to traverse array elements.
  • Passing addresses is a common way to return more than one result from a function.
  • Array elements can be accessed using pointer notation or index notation.
💬 Talk It Out

Why does swap() need pointers to actually work, instead of just passing the plain values?

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • C passes arguments by value; pointers are the only way for a function to modify a caller's variable.
  • An array name decays into a pointer to its first element when passed to a function.
  • arr[i] and *(arr + i) are interchangeable ways to access array elements via pointers.
  • A function receiving an array must also receive its size separately, since size information is not retained.
📝 Deep Dive

C always passes arguments by value, so a function normally cannot change the caller's variable directly — the only way to let a function modify a caller's variable (as swap does) is to pass a pointer to it, so the function can dereference and write through that address. When an array name is used in a function call, it automatically decays into a pointer to its first element, which is why arr[i] and *(arr + i) are interchangeable inside a function that receives an array parameter. This also explains why a function cannot determine the size of an array it receives — the size must be passed separately, as in findMax(arr, n) below.

🧩 Code Challenge

Write a function that receives an array (as a pointer) and its size, and returns the maximum value.

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
int findMax(int *arr, int n){
    int max = arr[0];
    for (int i = 1; i < n; i++)
        if (*(arr + i) > max) max = *(arr + i);
    return max;
}
int main(){
    int values[5] = {12, 45, 7, 89, 34};
    printf("Maximum = %d\n", findMax(values, 5));
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
Maximum = 89

Friday · 25 September 2026 · 8:00 AM - 10:00 AM

Address arithmetic; character pointers and functions

✨ The Vibe

Pointer arithmetic 'skipping' the right amount is like swiping through a photo carousel — the app always jumps exactly one photo-width at a time, never a random pixel.

📌 What you need to know
  • Pointer arithmetic depends on type size.
  • Character pointers are often used for strings.
  • String functions can be implemented with character pointers.
  • When a pointer moves to the next element, it advances by the size of the element type.
  • This is why integer pointers and character pointers move differently in memory.
💬 Talk It Out

Why would an int pointer and a char pointer move different amounts in memory for the exact same '+1'?

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • Pointer arithmetic is automatically scaled by the size of the type the pointer points to.
  • A C string is a char array ending in a null character '\0'.
  • String functions work by walking forward through memory until the null terminator is found.
  • Forgetting to leave room for, or overwriting, the null terminator is a classic source of bugs.
📝 Deep Dive

When you write p + 1 for a pointer, C automatically scales the addition by sizeof(*p) — for an int pointer this moves 4 bytes ahead, while for a char pointer it moves only 1 byte, even though both expressions look identical in source code. A C string is really just an array of characters ending in a special null character '\0', and every string function (including the strlen you will re-implement below) works by walking forward through memory until it finds that terminator. This null-terminator convention is exactly why forgetting to leave room for it (or overwriting it) is a classic source of string-handling bugs.

🧩 Code Challenge

Implement a custom strlen()-style function using only pointer arithmetic (no array indexing, no string.h).

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
int myStrlen(char *s){
    char *start = s;
    while (*s != '\0') s++;
    return s - start;
}
int main(){
    char text[] = "Hello";
    printf("Length = %d\n", myStrlen(text));
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
Length = 5

Pointer arrays (pointers to pointers)

✨ The Vibe

An array of strings is basically your phone's favorites list — it's really a list of shortcuts to full contact cards, not the entire cards crammed into one array.

📌 What you need to know
  • A pointer to a pointer stores another pointer.
  • This is used in dynamic and multi-level data structures.
  • It appears in advanced string and array handling.
  • Pointer-to-pointer structures are common in lists of strings.
  • The extra level of indirection allows flexible storage and access patterns.
💬 Talk It Out

Why is swapping two entries in a string array so cheap compared to swapping two whole paragraphs of actual text?

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • A pointer to a pointer (char **pp) stores the address of another pointer.
  • An array of strings (char *s[]) is really an array of pointers, each pointing to a string's first character.
  • argv in main(int argc, char *argv[]) is itself an array of pointers to argument strings.
  • Extra indirection allows flexible storage and access patterns for collections of pointers.
📝 Deep Dive

A pointer to a pointer (declared char **pp) stores the address of another pointer rather than the address of an ordinary value — dereferencing it once (*pp) gives you back that inner pointer, and dereferencing twice (**pp) gives you the value it eventually points to. This pattern is exactly how an array of strings (char *s[]) works internally: s is really an array of pointers, and s[i] is a char* pointing to the first character of the i-th string, which is why printing s[i] with %s works directly. The same idea extends naturally to argv in main(int argc, char *argv[]), which is itself an array of pointers to the command-line argument strings.

✨ The Vibe

A 2D array is basically a spreadsheet stored as one long scroll — row after row, back to back, with no gaps in between.

💬 Talk It Out

Sketch on paper how a 3x3 grid would get laid out as one straight line in memory.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • 2D arrays are stored in row-major order — all of row 0, then all of row 1, and so on.
  • The address of a[i][j] is base + (i * numColumns + j) * sizeof(type).
  • A function receiving a 2D array parameter must specify the number of columns.
  • Nested loops (rows outer, columns inner) are the standard pattern for visiting every matrix element.
📝 Deep Dive

C stores a 2D array in row-major order (Figure 10.1) — every element of row 0 comes first in memory, then every element of row 1, and so on — so the address of a[i][j] can always be computed as base + (i * numberOfColumns + j) * sizeof(type). This is why, when declaring a 2D array parameter in a function, the number of columns must always be specified (int f(int a[][3])) even though the number of rows can be left out — the compiler needs the column count to calculate offsets correctly. Nested loops (outer loop for rows, inner loop for columns) are the standard pattern for visiting every element of a matrix in order.

🧩 Code Challenge

Add two 2x2 matrices element-wise and print the resulting matrix (see Figure 10.1 for how the elements are laid out in memory).

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
int main(){
    int a[2][2] = {{1, 2}, {3, 4}};
    int b[2][2] = {{5, 6}, {7, 8}};
    int sum[2][2];
    for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++)
        for (int j = 0; j < 2; j++)
            sum[i][j] = a[i][j] + b[i][j];
    for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++){
        for (int j = 0; j < 2; j++) printf("%d ", sum[i][j]);
        printf("\n");
    }
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
6 8
10 12

Friday · 02 October 2026 · 8:00 AM - 10:00 AM

Pointers vs. multi-dimensional arrays; command-line arguments; pointers to functions

✨ The Vibe

Function pointers are like choosing which playlist algorithm runs based on your mood setting — same 'play music' action, completely different logic underneath.

📌 What you need to know
  • Arrays and pointer-based forms differ in memory behavior.
  • Command-line arguments allow inputs at program start.
  • Function pointers let programs choose behavior dynamically.
  • Command-line arguments are useful for automating input without interactive typing.
  • Function pointers are common in callback-style designs.
💬 Talk It Out

Where do apps you use let you 'plug in' different behavior like this — custom sort, custom filter, custom theme?

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • A true 2D array is one contiguous memory block; an array of row pointers is more flexible but not guaranteed contiguous.
  • argc counts command-line arguments (including the program name); argv holds the actual argument strings.
  • A function pointer stores the address of a function, letting a program choose behaviour at runtime.
  • Function pointers are the mechanism behind callback-style and table-driven designs.
📝 Deep Dive

A true 2D array (int a[2][2]) is one contiguous block of memory, while an array of pointers (int *a[2], each pointing to a separately allocated row) is more flexible (rows can have different lengths) but requires an extra level of dereferencing and is not guaranteed to be contiguous — the two are not interchangeable even though both use a[i][j] syntax. argc and argv in main(int argc, char *argv[]) let a program receive input directly from the command line when it starts, with argv[0] always being the program's own name and argc counting all arguments including that name. A function pointer (int (*op)(int,int)) stores the address of a function rather than data, letting a program choose which function to call at runtime — exactly the mechanism used to build the calculator below.

🧩 Code Challenge

Build a small calculator where an array of function pointers selects the operation (add, subtract, multiply).

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
int add(int a, int b){ return a + b; }
int sub(int a, int b){ return a - b; }
int mul(int a, int b){ return a * b; }
int main(){
    int (*ops[3])(int, int) = {add, sub, mul};
    const char *names[3] = {"add", "sub", "mul"};
    int a = 8, b = 3;
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++)
        printf("%s(%d, %d) = %d\n", names[i], a, b, ops[i](a, b));
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
add(8, 3) = 11
sub(8, 3) = 5
mul(8, 3) = 24

Monday · 05 October 2026 · 8:00 AM - 10:00 AM

Basics of structures

✨ The Vibe

A struct is a character sheet in a game — one named thing (the player) holding multiple related stats together (health, name, level) instead of scattered separately.

📌 What you need to know
  • Structures group related data together.
  • They are suitable for records such as students or books.
  • Each member can have a different type.
  • Structures are helpful when a single logical object contains many fields.
  • They improve clarity by representing a record as one named unit.
💬 Talk It Out

Design a struct out loud for your own 'gamer profile' — what fields would it actually need?

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • A struct groups several related members of possibly different types under one name.
  • Members are accessed with the dot operator (s.member).
  • A structure variable can be copied entirely to another with a simple assignment.
  • Structures are clearer than parallel arrays once a record has more than a few related fields.
📝 Deep Dive

A struct groups several related variables (called members) under one name, so a single Student variable can carry a roll number, a name, and marks together instead of needing three separate arrays kept in sync by index. Members are accessed with the dot operator (s.roll), and the whole structure can be copied to another variable of the same type with a simple assignment (struct Student s2 = s1;), which copies every member at once. Choosing a structure over several parallel arrays is almost always clearer once a record has more than two or three related fields, because it keeps each entity's data physically grouped together.

struct Employee{ int id; char name[20]; float salary; };

    struct Employee e = {101, "Priya", 55000.0f};
    printf("Book: %s by %s, Rs.%.2f\n", b.title, b.author, b.price);
    printf("Employee: %d %s Rs.%.2f\n", e.id, e.name, e.salary);
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
Book: The C Programming Language by K&R, Rs.450.00
Employee: 101 Priya Rs.55000.00

Tuesday · 06 October 2026 · 2:00 PM - 4:00 PM

Structures and functions; arrays of structures

✨ The Vibe

Passing a struct by value into a function is like sending someone a screenshot of your profile — they can look at it, even mark it up, but your real profile stays untouched.

📌 What you need to know
  • Structures can be passed to functions.
  • Arrays of structures store multiple records.
  • This pattern is common in management programs.
  • Functions can accept whole structures when the record size is manageable.
  • Arrays of structures are useful for lists, registers, and databases.
💬 Talk It Out

Why would you use a pointer instead of a copy if you actually wanted a function to permanently update your profile?

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • Passing a structure by value gives the function a full copy; changes inside do not affect the caller's original.
  • An array of structures (struct Student list[50]) represents a table of records naturally.
  • list[i] gives a complete record; list[i].field gives one field of that record.
  • For large structures, or to allow in-place modification, pass a pointer instead of the whole structure.
📝 Deep Dive

When a structure is passed to a function by value (as show(struct Student s) does), the function receives a full copy — changes made inside the function do not affect the caller's original structure, exactly like passing an int or float by value. For larger structures, or when the function needs to modify the original, a pointer to the structure (Friday's topic) is used instead to avoid copying and to allow in-place updates. An array of structures (struct Student list[50]) is the natural way to represent a table of records, where list[i] gives you the i-th complete record and list[i].marks gives you one field of that record.

    };

        printf("%d %-6s %.2f\n", list[i].roll, list[i].name, list[i].marks);
    return 0;
}

2 Ana    92.00

Friday · 09 October 2026 · 8:00 AM - 10:00 AM

Pointers to structures

✨ The Vibe

The arrow operator (->) is just 'go to this address, then check this one stat' in a single move — a shortcut instead of two separate steps.

📌 What you need to know
  • A pointer to a structure allows member access through ->.
  • It is useful when passing large records to functions.
  • It improves flexibility in dynamic programs.
  • The arrow operator combines dereferencing and member access.
  • Pointers to structures are common in linked data representations.
💬 Talk It Out

Walk a partner through why p->roll and (*p).roll mean the exact same thing.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • A pointer to a structure allows member access through the arrow operator (p->member).
  • p->member is exactly equivalent to (*p).member.
  • Passing a structure pointer avoids copying and lets a function modify the original data.
  • This pointer-to-structure pattern is the foundation for linked lists and trees studied later.
📝 Deep Dive

Given struct Student *p = &s;, the expression p->roll is exactly equivalent to (*p).roll — the arrow operator exists purely as a convenient shorthand so you do not have to write the dereference and the dot separately. Passing a pointer to a structure into a function (instead of the structure itself) avoids copying the whole record and, crucially, lets the function's changes be seen by the caller, which is why update-style functions in real programs almost always take a struct pointer rather than a struct by value. This same pointer-to-structure pattern is the foundation for linked lists and trees in later data structures courses, where each node is a structure containing a pointer to the next node.

🧩 Code Challenge

Use a structure pointer to update a student's marks and print the value before and after the change.

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
struct Student{ int roll; float marks; };
int main(){
    struct Student s = {5, 60.0f};
    struct Student *p = &s;
    printf("Before: %.2f\n", p->marks);
    p->marks += 5.0f;   // grace marks added through the pointer
    printf("After : %.2f\n", p->marks);
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
Before: 60.00
After : 65.00

Exp 12 Table Lookup, typedef, Unions, and Bit-Fields CO3
Monday · 12 October 2026 · 8:00 AM - 10:00 AM

Table lookup

✨ The Vibe

A lookup table is your phone's autocomplete — instead of 'figuring out' the word every single time, it instantly looks up the answer from a pre-built list.

📌 What you need to know
  • Lookup tables replace repeated conditions with stored results.
  • They are useful for quick mapping tasks.
  • They improve readability when the mapping is fixed.
  • A lookup table saves time when the same mapping is used many times.
  • It is a compact alternative to long chains of if-else statements.
💬 Talk It Out

Name an app feature that's basically a lookup table under the hood — emoji suggestions, autofill, predictive text.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • A lookup table stores pre-computed answers to a fixed mapping in an array for instant retrieval.
  • Table lookups replace long if-else/else-if ladders with a single indexed access.
  • This technique works best when the input can be mapped to a small, predictable array index.
  • The trade-off is memory (to store the table) for speed and readability.
📝 Deep Dive

A table lookup stores the answers to a fixed mapping in an array (or similar structure) ahead of time, so the program can retrieve a result with a single indexed access instead of testing many conditions one by one — this becomes especially valuable as the number of cases grows, since a long else-if ladder is both slower to read and slower to maintain than one array lookup. The technique works best when the mapping's input can be turned into a small, predictable array index, such as a month number 1-12 or a grade letter's ASCII position. The trade-off is memory for speed and clarity: the table itself must be stored, but the lookup itself is nearly instantaneous and the code reads naturally as 'look up the answer' rather than 'work out the answer'.

🧩 Code Challenge

        "January", "February", "March", "April", "May", "June",
        "July", "August", "September", "October", "November", "December"
    };
    int monthNumber = 8;
    printf("Month %d is %s\n", monthNumber, months[monthNumber - 1]);
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
Month 8 is August

Tuesday · 13 October 2026 · 2:00 PM - 4:00 PM

typedef and unions

✨ The Vibe

A union is like one storage locker that can hold your gym bag OR your backpack, never both at once — whatever you stuffed in last is all that's actually usable.

📌 What you need to know
  • typedef creates type aliases.
  • A union stores different members in the same memory.
  • Only one union member should be meaningfully used at a time.
  • typedef reduces repetition in type names and improves readability.
  • Unions are memory-efficient when only one value is needed at a time.
💬 Talk It Out

Why is a union risky if you're not careful about tracking which 'item' you last stored in it?

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • typedef creates a shorter alias for a type, purely for readability with no effect on memory layout.
  • A union's members all share the same memory; its size equals its largest member's size.
  • Only one union member holds a meaningful value at any given time.
  • Unions save memory for 'one value, multiple possible types' scenarios, at the cost of needing to track the active member.
📝 Deep Dive

typedef struct {...} Name; creates a shorter alias so you can write Name variable; instead of repeating struct Name variable; every time — purely a readability convenience with no effect on memory layout. A union looks exactly like a structure syntactically, but all of its members share the same block of memory (Figure 12.1), so the union's total size equals the size of its largest member, not the sum of all members as with a structure. This makes unions memory-efficient for representing 'one value that could be one of several types' (for example, a generic data cell that is sometimes an int and sometimes a float), but the programmer must keep track of which member was last written, since writing one member and then reading a different one gives meaningless results.

🧩 Code Challenge

Print sizeof for an equivalent struct and union (Figure 12.1) to show the memory difference directly.

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
typedef struct{ int i; float f; } DataStruct;
typedef union{ int i; float f; } DataUnion;
int main(){
    printf("sizeof(DataStruct) = %zu bytes\n", sizeof(DataStruct));
    printf("sizeof(DataUnion)  = %zu bytes\n", sizeof(DataUnion));
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
sizeof(DataStruct) = 8 bytes
sizeof(DataUnion)  = 4 bytes

Friday · 16 October 2026 · 8:00 AM - 10:00 AM

Bit-fields

✨ The Vibe

Bit-fields are like packing for a carry-on-only trip — squeezing several small things into the tiniest space possible instead of using a whole suitcase per item.

📌 What you need to know
  • Bit-fields pack information into a few bits.
  • They are useful for flags and compact storage.
  • Layout can vary across compilers.
  • Bit-fields are a low-level optimization for saving memory.
  • They are frequently used in flag-related records and status values.
💬 Talk It Out

Where would tightly packing data like this actually matter in a real device — a smartwatch, a fitness tracker, a smart sensor?

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • Bit-fields let a structure reserve an exact number of bits for a member, packing several flags tightly.
  • This is most useful for status registers, permission flags, or similar compact boolean-style data.
  • Exact bit ordering and layout can vary between compilers and platforms.
  • Bit-fields trade a small amount of access overhead for meaningful memory savings at scale.
📝 Deep Dive

A bit-field declared as unsigned int flag : 1; tells the compiler to reserve only 1 bit for that member instead of a full 4-byte int, which lets several small flags be packed together tightly inside one machine word. This is most useful for status registers or permission flags, where a program might need dozens of independent true/false values and packing them saves noticeable memory at scale (for example, in embedded systems or network packet headers). The exact bit ordering and total storage used by a bit-field structure can vary between compilers and platforms, so bit-fields are best treated as a memory-saving convenience rather than a way to guarantee a specific binary layout across different machines.

🧩 Code Challenge

Model file permissions (read, write, execute) as a 3-bit bit-field structure and print the flags.

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
struct Permissions{
    unsigned int read  : 1;
    unsigned int write : 1;
    unsigned int exec  : 1;
};
int main(){
    struct Permissions p = {1, 1, 0};   // read+write, no execute
    printf("read=%u write=%u exec=%u\n", p.read, p.write, p.exec);
    printf("Size of Permissions = %zu byte(s)\n", sizeof(p));
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
read=1 write=1 exec=0
Size of Permissions = 4 byte(s)
