Exp 13 Basics of AI-Assisted Coding CO5
Monday · 19 October 2026 · 8:00 AM - 10:00 AM

Basics of AI-assisted coding using GitHub Copilot / CodiumAI

✨ The Vibe

Trusting AI-generated code without checking it is like posting the first draft of a caption with zero proofreading — it might look fine at a glance and still be dead wrong.

📌 What you need to know
  • AI tools help generate code and explanations.
  • They are best used as assistants, not replacements.
  • Human review remains essential.
  • Good AI-assisted coding still requires understanding the problem first.
  • Always verify whether the generated code is safe, correct, and readable.
💬 Talk It Out

Share a time any AI tool confidently gave you a wrong answer. How did you actually catch it?

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • AI coding assistants suggest plausible code based on learned patterns, not provably correct code.
  • Write or sketch the intended logic yourself first, then use AI suggestions as an accelerant, not a substitute.
  • Always compile, run, and review AI-generated code before trusting it.
  • Security-sensitive code deserves extra scrutiny since AI training data can contain insecure patterns.
📝 Deep Dive

AI coding assistants like GitHub Copilot or CodiumAI suggest code based on patterns learned from large amounts of existing code, which means they can produce syntactically correct but subtly wrong or inefficient solutions — they predict plausible code, not necessarily provably correct code. The safest workflow is: write (or at least sketch) the logic yourself first so you understand the intended approach, then use the AI suggestion as a faster way to type it out or as a second opinion, always followed by your own review and testing. Because these tools are trained on public code, they can also occasionally reproduce insecure patterns (like unchecked buffer sizes in C), so security-relevant code deserves extra scrutiny before it is trusted.

🧩 Code Challenge

Ask an AI assistant to generate a C function that checks if a number is prime, then verify it by hand-tracing two test cases.

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
int isPrime(int n){
    if (n < 2) return 0;
    for (int i = 2; i * i <= n; i++)
        if (n % i == 0) return 0;
    return 1;
}
int main(){
    printf("7 is prime: %d\n", isPrime(7));
    printf("9 is prime: %d\n", isPrime(9));
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
7 is prime: 1
9 is prime: 0

Verification: for n=9 the loop tests i=2 (9%2!=0) then i=3 (9%3==0) so it correctly returns 0 (not prime) — always hand-trace at least one true and one false case before trusting AI-generated code.

Tuesday · 20 October 2026 · 2:00 PM - 4:00 PM

Prompting and workflow practice

✨ The Vibe

A vague prompt is like asking a friend to 'grab me food' with zero details — you might get exactly what you didn't want. A specific prompt is like sending the exact order link.

📌 What you need to know
  • Specific prompts lead to better results.
  • The workflow should include review and correction.
  • Prompt quality affects output quality.
  • A good prompt states the language, goal, constraints, and expected behavior.
  • The final code should be tested by the student, not just copied.
💬 Talk It Out

In pairs, rewrite a vague prompt into a specific one for any coding task you can think of.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • A strong prompt states the language, the exact goal, constraints, and a test case to verify success.
  • Iterative prompting (asking follow-up questions) is usually more productive than one giant prompt.
  • Whatever the AI produces, always compile, test, and read it before using it.
  • Vague prompts force the AI to guess details, producing less reliable results.
📝 Deep Dive

A strong prompt for code generation typically states four things explicitly: the language (C), the exact goal (what the function should compute), any constraints (input range, performance, style rules from class), and how you will know it worked (a sample input and expected output). Iterative prompting — asking a follow-up like 'now handle the case where the array is empty' — is usually more productive than trying to write one giant, perfect prompt up front. Whatever the AI produces, the workflow always ends the same way: compile it, run it against your own test cases, and read it line by line before it goes into an assignment or project.

🧩 Code Challenge

Compare a vague prompt versus a specific prompt for the same task, and note the difference in usefulness.

Tap to reveal the solution

Vague prompt: 'write code to sort numbers' — the AI must guess the language, input format, and sort order. Specific prompt: 'write a C function that takes an int array and its size, and sorts it in ascending order using bubble sort, with a main() that tests it on {5,1,4,2,3}' — this states language, goal, method, and a concrete test case, so the generated code can be verified immediately against the expected sorted output {1,2,3,4,5}.

Mini review and application

✨ The Vibe

Treat AI output like a rough draft from a groupmate — genuinely useful, but you still review it carefully before it goes anywhere near your final submission.

📌 What you need to know
  • Use AI output carefully and verify correctness.
  • Refine generated code for readability and safety.
  • Treat AI as a drafting helper.
  • Compare generated solutions with what you learned in class.
  • Ask the tool to explain code, not just write it.
💬 Talk It Out

What's your personal rule going to be for how much you trust AI-generated code for the rest of this course?

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • Ask an AI assistant to explain its own code — a mismatched explanation often signals a bug or unnecessary complexity.
  • Comparing AI output against class-taught approaches reinforces the underlying concept.
  • By this stage, treat AI suggestions like advice from a classmate: helpful, but always checked.
  • Refining AI output for clarity is itself a valuable skill, not just accepting the first draft.
📝 Deep Dive

A useful habit is to ask the AI assistant to explain its own generated code line by line — if the explanation does not match what you understand the code to do, that mismatch is often a sign of a bug or of code that is more complicated than necessary. Comparing an AI-generated solution against the approach taught in class (for example, comparing an AI's string-reversal one-liner against the pointer-based version from Experiment 9) reinforces the underlying concept rather than just producing working code. By this stage of the course, you should be comfortable treating AI suggestions the same way you would treat a suggestion from a classmate: helpful, but always checked against your own understanding before it is trusted.

🧩 Code Challenge

Take an AI-suggested one-liner for reversing a string and rewrite it as clear, well-commented C code matching class style.

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
void reverseString(char *s){
    int left = 0;
    int right = strlen(s) - 1;
    while (left < right){
        char temp = s[left];
        s[left] = s[right];
        s[right] = temp;
        left++;
        right--;
    }
}
int main(){
    char text[] = "PPS1";
    reverseString(text);
    printf("%s\n", text);
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
1SPP

Exp 14 Code Comprehension Using AI-Generated Code CO4 · CO5
Monday · 26 October 2026 · 8:00 AM - 10:00 AM

Reading AI-generated code

✨ The Vibe

Reading unfamiliar AI code is like reading a group project doc someone else already wrote — you trace who's doing what before you touch anything.

📌 What you need to know
  • Understand the code before changing it.
  • AI-generated code can be syntactically correct but unclear.
  • Line-by-line reading improves confidence.
  • Look for variable roles, control flow, and data movement.
  • If the code is not clear, rewrite it in a simpler form.
💬 Talk It Out

Read a partner's AI-generated snippet out loud and narrate what each variable is actually 'doing' as you go.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • Identify each variable's role (counter, accumulator, flag, index) before judging what code does.
  • Trace control flow (loops and conditions) before worrying about small syntax details.
  • AI-generated code sometimes favors compact constructs over clarity.
  • Annotating unfamiliar code with your own comments builds real understanding, not just recognition.
📝 Deep Dive

When reading unfamiliar code, first identify the role of each variable (is it a counter, an accumulator, a flag, or an index?), then trace the control flow (which loops and conditions the program passes through) before worrying about small syntax details. AI-generated code sometimes favors compact or 'clever' constructs over clarity, so a good comprehension habit is to mentally (or literally) rewrite a dense line into two or three simpler lines and confirm they behave the same way. Annotating unfamiliar code with your own comments, as in the example below, is one of the fastest ways to convert 'I can see what this does' into 'I understand why this works'.

🧩 Code Challenge

Read an unfamiliar AI-generated snippet that counts vowels in a string and annotate what each line does.

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
int main(){
    char s[] = "Programming";
    int count = 0;                       // running total of vowels
    for (int i = 0; s[i] != '\0'; i++){  // walk the string until the null terminator
        char c = s[i];
        if (c=='a'||c=='e'||c=='i'||c=='o'||c=='u'||
            c=='A'||c=='E'||c=='I'||c=='O'||c=='U')
            count++;                      // matched a vowel, increase the count
    }
    printf("Vowels = %d\n", count);      // report the final count
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
Vowels = 3

Tuesday · 27 October 2026 · 2:00 PM - 4:00 PM

Checking correctness and edge cases

✨ The Vibe

Testing edge cases on AI code is like stress-testing a Discord bot before deploying it to your whole server — you want to know what breaks it before your friends do.

📌 What you need to know
  • Test expected and boundary inputs.
  • Edge cases reveal hidden bugs.
  • Review logic carefully before trusting output.
  • Edge cases include zero, negative values, empty input, and large input.
  • A good tester asks what can go wrong, not only what should go right.
💬 Talk It Out

As a group, list the weirdest edge case you can think of for any function discussed this week.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • Always test zero, empty, negative, and boundary inputs, not just typical cases.
  • AI-generated code is just as capable of missing edge cases as human-written code.
  • Finding an edge case that breaks a function is the testing process succeeding, not failing.
  • The same normal/boundary/invalid testing discipline from Experiment 5 applies to any code, AI-generated or not.
📝 Deep Dive

A systematic edge-case checklist for almost any function includes: what happens with zero or an empty collection, what happens with the smallest and largest values the input is allowed to take, what happens with negative numbers if the function was designed with only positives in mind, and what happens if the input is exactly at a boundary condition (such as marks equal to exactly 40 for a pass/fail cutoff). AI-generated code is just as capable of missing these cases as human-written code, so the testing discipline from Experiment 5 (test normal, boundary, and invalid cases) applies with equal force here. Finding an edge case that breaks a function is not a failure of the exercise — it is the exercise succeeding at its job of catching a real bug before it reaches production.

🧩 Code Challenge

Test an AI-generated average() function against normal, zero-length, and negative-number edge cases.

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
float average(int arr[], int n){
    if (n == 0) return 0.0f;   // guard against division by zero
    int total = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) total += arr[i];
    return (float)total / n;
}
int main(){
    int normal[3] = {10, 20, 30};
    int negatives[3] = {-5, 5, 0};
    printf("average(normal) = %.2f\n", average(normal, 3));
    printf("average(negatives) = %.2f\n", average(negatives, 3));
    printf("average(empty) = %.2f\n", average(normal, 0));
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
average(normal) = 20.00
average(negatives) = 0.00
average(empty) = 0.00

Without the 'if (n == 0)' guard, the empty-input case would divide by zero — this is exactly the kind of edge case a first reading of AI-generated code can miss.

  2. Test an AI-generated factorial function against an input of 0 and a negative input, and decide what the correct behaviour should be for the negative case.
  3. Write down three edge cases you would test for a function that checks whether a given year is a leap year.

Friday · 30 October 2026 · 8:00 AM - 10:00 AM

Improving AI-generated code

✨ The Vibe

Refactoring AI code for clarity is like editing a rough voice-to-text transcript into something that actually reads well.

📌 What you need to know
  • Simplify logic where possible.
  • Use better names and comments.
  • Refactor for readability and correctness.
  • Improvement can also mean removing unnecessary complexity.
  • The best output is understandable to a human reader.
💬 Talk It Out

Take a confusing one-liner as a group and vote on the clearest possible rewrite.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • Refactoring changes how code is written without changing what it does.
  • Rename cryptic variables and add comments explaining base cases and key decisions.
  • Breaking a dense expression into simpler statements improves readability without changing behaviour.
  • Treat every AI-generated snippet you plan to keep as a draft that deserves a final readability pass.
📝 Deep Dive

Refactoring means changing how code is written without changing what it does — the corrected power function below produces exactly the same results as the cryptic one-liner it replaces, but a human reader can follow it on first read. Good refactors usually involve renaming cryptic variables (x, y become base, exponent), adding a comment at the base case explaining why it is the base case, and breaking a single dense expression into two or three simpler statements. Treat every piece of AI-generated code that you plan to keep as a draft: the final step is always to make it read the way you would want a teammate to hand it to you.

🧩 Code Challenge

Refactor a cryptic one-line AI-generated power function into a clear, well-named, commented version.

Tap to reveal the solution 
// Before (AI-generated, hard to read):
// int p(int x,int y){return y==0?1:x*p(x,y-1);}

// After (refactored for clarity):
#include <stdio.h>
int power(int base, int exponent){
    if (exponent == 0) return 1;         // base case: anything^0 = 1
    return base * power(base, exponent - 1);
}
int main(){
    printf("2^5 = %d\n", power(2, 5));
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
2^5 = 32
🎯 Try These On Your Own

  2. Refactor an AI-generated loop that uses single-letter variable names (i, j, k, t) into one with descriptive names, without changing its behaviour.
  3. Take any solved example from an earlier experiment and identify one small readability improvement you could make to it.

Mini project planning and topic finalization

✨ The Vibe

Planning your mini project is drafting your pitch before you start building — scope it like a group video project: who does what, how long it'll take, what's actually realistic.

📌 What you need to know
  • Choose a manageable problem statement.
  • Define scope, inputs, outputs, and modules.
  • Plan the work before implementation.
  • A clear topic avoids confusion later in the semester.
  • The project should be small enough to complete but rich enough to demonstrate concepts.
💬 Talk It Out

Pitch your mini project idea to your group in 30 seconds flat — no more, no less.

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • Choose a project topic that naturally uses several concepts from the semester together.
  • Plan scope, inputs, outputs, and modules before writing any code, exactly as in Experiment 2.
  • A realistic, well-tested scope demonstrates more understanding than an ambitious, unfinished one.
  • Sketching the menu and module list up front avoids confusion later in the project.
📝 Deep Dive

A good mini-project topic for this course is one that naturally uses at least three or four concepts from the semester — for example, a Student Record Management system uses structures (Experiment 11), arrays of structures (Experiment 11), functions (Experiment 5), and a switch-based menu (Experiment 4) all together. Before writing any code, write down the plan exactly the way you would in Experiment 2: inputs, outputs, constraints, and the list of sub-problems (modules) the project breaks into. Keeping the scope realistic (a handful of well-tested modules) is far more valuable for demonstrating understanding than an ambitious project that is left half-working.

Tuesday · 03 November 2026 · 2:00 PM - 4:00 PM

Mini project implementation

✨ The Vibe

Build one module, test it, then move to the next — exactly like editing one scene of a video before touching the next one, instead of filming everything and editing it all at once at the end.

📌 What you need to know
  • Build the project in small stages.
  • Test each module as it is completed.
  • Keep the code readable and documented.
  • Integration should happen after each module works individually.
  • Good project work includes version control and regular backup of files.
💬 Talk It Out

What's your team's backup plan if a teammate's module isn't working the day before it's due?

🔑 Key Takeaways
  • Implement and test one function at a time rather than writing everything at once.
  • Confirm each module works correctly before moving on to the next.
  • Keep a simple backup habit before making large changes to working code.
  • Integration should happen only after each individual module is verified.
📝 Deep Dive

Implement and test one function at a time — write addStudent(), call it a few times with a temporary main() and print the results, and only move on to displayAll() once you are confident the data is being stored correctly. This 'build one piece, test it, then move to the next' rhythm is far less error-prone than writing the entire program at once and debugging everything together at the end. Keep a simple backup habit (copying the file with a date in its name, or using git if you know it) before making any large change, so a broken experiment can always be rolled back to the last known-working version.

🧩 Code Challenge

Implement and test the addStudent() and displayAll() modules from the plan in isolation before integrating the full menu.

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
struct Student{ int roll; char name[20]; float marks; };
struct Student list[50];
int count = 0;
void addStudent(int roll, const char *name, float marks){
    list[count].roll = roll;
    snprintf(list[count].name, 20, "%s", name);
    list[count].marks = marks;
    count++;
}
void displayAll(void){
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++)
        printf("%d %s %.2f\n", list[i].roll, list[i].name, list[i].marks);
}
int main(){
    addStudent(1, "Ram", 88.0f);
    addStudent(2, "Ana", 91.5f);
    displayAll();
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
1 Ram 88.00
2 Ana 91.50

Mini project testing, debugging, and presentation

✨ The Vibe

Presenting your project is just like presenting a portfolio piece — show the process, not just the final result, and be ready for the 'why did you build it that way' follow-up.

📌 What you need to know
  • Testing confirms that requirements are met.
  • Debugging fixes problems found during execution.

📝 Deep Dive

Before presenting, run through every requirement from your Monday plan and confirm each one is actually met, including edge cases like searching for a roll number that does not exist (as tested below). A good presentation follows the same input-process-output structure used throughout this course: show what data goes in, briefly explain how each module processes it, and show the final output, rather than reading through the source code line by line. Anticipate two or three likely viva questions about your design choices (for example, 'why did you use an array of structures instead of separate arrays?') and prepare short, confident answers grounded in what you learned in the relevant experiment.

🧩 Code Challenge

Add and test a searchByRoll() module, including the 'not found' edge case, to complete the mini project's core functionality.

Tap to reveal the solution 
#include <stdio.h>
struct Student{ int roll; char name[20]; float marks; };
struct Student list[2] = {{1, "Ram", 88.0f}, {2, "Ana", 91.5f}};
void searchByRoll(int roll){
    for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++){
        if (list[i].roll == roll){
            printf("Found: %s, %.2f\n", list[i].name, list[i].marks);
            return;
        }
    }
    printf("Roll number %d not found\n", roll);
}
int main(){
    searchByRoll(2);
    searchByRoll(9);
    return 0;
}
Expected output:
Found: Ana, 91.50
Roll number 9 not found
